name: Transition Planning
title: Transition Planning
answer: Transition planning is the part of a student's IEP that prepares them for life after high school, covering further education, work, and independent living, and federal rules require it in the IEP in effect when the student turns 16, though states and districts may begin earlier. AI can support the team by researching careers, training programs, and support services, but the student's own goals and voice must drive the plan.

sections.body: Transition planning is the process that gets students with disabilities ready for life after high school, including further education, work, and independent living. Federal regulations require it in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16, and states may start earlier, with many districts beginning at 14. The plan is meant to reflect the student's own goals and interests rather than a standard set of options. AI can help teams gather information about careers, training programs, and support services so that planning is better informed. The problem it solves is that transition options are wide and hard to research well, and a tool can widen the picture while the student and team keep control of the decisions.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher can use an approved tool, with names removed, to research options that match a student's interests and strengths. The student then explores those options and talks them over with the team and family, and the plan is built around what the student wants. Students should lead their transition planning as much as possible, and some can use AI tools to research careers, practice interview questions, or draft a letter to an employer, with support. These are real skills they will need after high school. The team makes sure the student's voice, not the tool's suggestions, drives the plan. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond the age thresholds for when planning must or may begin.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice and on the legal requirement it cites rather than on research evidence. The one authority it names is the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act regulations at 34 C.F.R. § 300.320, which require transition planning in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16, with states permitted to start earlier and many districts beginning at 14.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits in the text are about who stays in charge. AI is used only to gather information, and any tool must be approved and used with names removed. The student explores the options and discusses them with the team and family, and the plan is built around what the student wants. When students use AI to research careers, practice interviews, or draft a letter to an employer, they do so with support. The team's job is to ensure the student's voice, not the tool's suggestions, drives the plan.
